The plan is clear, but several internal inconsistencies and analytical gaps undermine credibility. Priority fixes:

1) Resolve factual contradictions. The plan says it has 'registered the company' and also that it 'has not yet formed a legal entity.' State one accurate status. It also describes payments, deposits and verified university accounts as core features, yet the funding ask includes $10,000 to build in-app payments, damage protection and verified onboarding. Clarify what exists in the pilot versus what is planned, and how pilot payments were actually handled.

2) Fix market sizing. The TAM math is off: 19M students x $100-150 gives roughly $1.9B-$2.85B, but the plan applies this to all students while claiming 3-4 events a year, and it treats spend on purchases as the addressable market even though the product substitutes lower-priced rentals (and a 70% saving shrinks revenue per user). Do bottom-up sizing instead: students x rentals per year x average order x fee rate. The '5% capture exceeds $50M' claim is also muddled, since 5% of a $2-3B market is $100-150M of spending, not the serviceable 6M-student base, and the take rate on that volume (about $7M of fees) is the number investors care about. Report GMV and net revenue separately.

3) Reconcile unit economics and forecasts. Fee revenue is stated as $4.65 per rental (15% of $31), but 63 renters generating $1,940 implies about 63 rentals at $31 and $291 in fees; confirm whether this is renters or rentals and whether the 44% repeat figure is meaningful on a six-week sample of 28 people. The 12-month forecast ($55K GMV, $9K fees) is tiny against the $25K ask and a 4-campus rollout; show per-campus assumptions, conversion from registered users to renters (pilot: 63/187, about 34%), seasonality, and cost lines. Claims such as 'break-even on direct costs' and 'low acquisition cost' need numbers: ambassador costs, payment processing fees (roughly 3% will erode a 15% fee), insurance, and damage/loss costs against the $2 waiver.

4) Address the core marketplace risks head-on. Supply-demand liquidity (241 listings but only 63 renters), repeated use of the same few popular items, cleaning and hygiene, damage and non-return liability, size and fit coverage, and seasonality that leaves long dead periods are all underexplored. Explain the damage deposit mechanics, who bears loss, dispute resolution, and fraud prevention. Quantify pilot learnings: listing-to-rental conversion, damage incidents, return rate, time to match.

5) Strengthen evidence and tighten claims. The survey of 412 respondents is cited without sampling method, bias, or willingness-to-rent data; add stated and revealed willingness to pay. 'Hyperlocal trust layer' and 'hard to copy' defenses are asserted, not demonstrated; show why campus density and org partnerships are defensible, and name specific competitors (Rent the Runway, Poshmark, campus swap groups) with a comparison. Also state the single-campus pilot's limits: it is one school with one cultural context, so say what you will test to prove repeatability.

6) Improve structure and specificity of the ask. Tie each use of funds to a measurable milestone (e.g., 'reach X renters per campus and Y% repeat rate by date Z'), define success metrics for the seed raise, and address team gaps: no one has marketplace-operations, trust-and-safety or legal experience, and all three are students with competing time commitments, so state commitment level, advisors, and equity split. Cut promotional phrasing and replace it with evidence.
